summary: This informational document refines the reference models for the user-to-network and network-to-network interfaces in MPLS Transport Profile networks. It updates models from the MPLS-TP framework of RFC 5921 by showing more detailed reference points and clarifying the interfaces.

plainLanguage.summary: In a phone company's network there are plugs where customers connect and where networks connect to each other. This draws a clearer map of those plugs.

questions: what is the difference between uni and nni
subtitle: Redrawn reference models that show exactly where the customer-facing and network-facing interfaces sit in an MPLS-TP network.

tldr.problem: The MPLS-TP framework in RFC 5921 drew the User-to-Network Interface (UNI) and Network-to-Network Interface (NNI) as spans, although the convention is to show interfaces as reference points.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6215 replaces those figures with detailed ones that mark reference points, split the UNI into client-side (UNI-C) and network-side (UNI-N) functions, and add a few terms.
tldr.outcome: It makes no other changes: it is an informational clarification that updates RFC 5921 and introduces no new security considerations.

today: RFC 6215 is an Informational RFC published in April 2011 that updates RFC 5921, and it has not been obsoleted. Its figures stand in place of the corresponding ones in RFC 5921.

sections.title: What This Document Updates
sections.content:
The framework for MPLS in transport networks, RFC 5921, gives reference models for the two Transport Service Interfaces of the MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP): a User-to-Network Interface (UNI) and a Network-to-Network Interface (NNI). RFC 6215 updates those models to show detailed reference points and to clarify the functional architecture of MPLS-TP at a UNI and an NNI.

The old figures drew the UNI and NNI as spans between nodes. The RFC points out that the convention is to draw interfaces as reference points. For the UNI it is also useful to show how the functions are shared between the Customer Edge (CE) side and the Provider Edge (PE) side. The new illustrations obsolete the matching ones in RFC 5921, and the document states that no other updates are made.

It is a product of a joint IETF and ITU-T effort to bring an MPLS Transport Profile into the IETF MPLS and PWE3 architectures, supporting the capabilities of a packet transport network as defined by the ITU-T.
sections.plainLanguage: The old picture drew a doorway as a long squiggle. The new picture draws it as a clear spot and shows which side of the door belongs to the customer and which to the network company.

sections.title: Terms and Layers
sections.content:
The terminology of RFC 5921 applies. RFC 6215 adds CP (Control Plane), NNI, TSI, UNI, UNI-C (the client side of the UNI) and UNI-N (the network side of the UNI).

A Transport Service Instance (TSI) is a single logical point-to-point connection at the Transport Service layer. It runs between the ingress PE that provides a packet transport service to a CE and the matching egress PE to which the peer CE is attached.

Only PE nodes need to know about the Transport Service layer, so only PEs appear in the figures. Provider (P) nodes need no awareness of it. Both PE and P nodes take part in the Transport Path layer. A PE terminates the transport paths it supports, acting as a Label Edge Router (LER), and multiplexes and demultiplexes Transport Service Instance traffic over those paths.
sections.plainLanguage: A TSI is like a private pipe between two customers' doors. Only the stations at the ends need to know about the pipe; the stations in the middle just pass the traffic along.

sections.title: The User-to-Network Interface
sections.content:
Figure 1 of the RFC, which obsoletes Figure 3 of RFC 5921, shows a UNI between a Customer Edge node and an MPLS-TP Provider Edge node. The UNI is split into a UNI-C function on the customer side and a UNI-N function on the network side.

Each side holds a signaling controller and client or service traffic processing. A control channel joins the two signaling controllers, and client traffic flows pass between the traffic processing blocks over a data link. On the PE, a client service control block and a transport path mux/demux function connect to the transport paths and the TSIs of the MPLS-TP network.

The RFC stresses that the term "MPLS-TP UNI" means a UNI to an MPLS-TP network. It does not name the protocol that crosses the UNI. Signaling between CE and PE may be used for a particular client flow, and if it is, it may travel over the same attachment circuit as the client flow. The client service control plane may be a control protocol of the native service, or GMPLS.
sections.plainLanguage: At the customer's door there are two helpers, one on each side, who talk to each other and pass the customer's packages through. Which helper does what is now clearly drawn.

sections.title: The Network-to-Network Interface
sections.content:
Figure 2, which obsoletes Figure 5 of RFC 5921, shows an NNI between MPLS-TP Provider Edge Node A and Provider Edge Node B. Each node has an NNI function, and the figure shows a Transport Service control plane and a Transport Path control plane, each with its own signaling controller and a control channel to its peer.

On the data plane, each node has transport service processing and a transport path mux/demux. The transport path between the two nodes carries the Transport Service Instances (TSIs) across the interface.

For a particular Transport Service Instance, the NNI may involve signaling between the two PEs. If signaling is used, it may travel over the same data link that supports the service instance.
sections.plainLanguage: Where two network companies meet, each has a door, a signaling helper and a package handler. The helpers chat, and the packages ride a shared road between the two companies.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of RFC 5921 apply. The updated reference models in RFC 6215 introduce no new security considerations, which fits with a document that only redraws figures and adds terms.
sections.plainLanguage: Redrawing a map does not change who can walk through the doors, so nothing new needs guarding.
